5.2 Explain elements of the risk management process
A storage vendor's datasheet says a drive model averages 1.2 million hours of operation before it fails. Which metric is this?
Mean time between failures measures average operating time before failure, an indicator of reliability.
MTTR is repair time, RTO is a recovery target, and ARO is how often a risk event is expected per year.
5.3 Explain the processes associated with third-party risk assessment and management

Before signing with a SaaS provider that will hold customer data, a company wants a contractual guarantee that it can inspect the provider's security controls, or have a third party do so, if concerns arise. What clause should it negotiate?
A right-to-audit clause gives the customer the contractual right to audit the vendor's controls, directly or through a third party.
Non-compete, termination, and force majeure clauses address other contractual matters.
5.3 Explain the processes associated with third-party risk assessment and management

A hosting contract commits the provider to 99.9% monthly uptime and a four-hour response time for critical incidents, with service credits if it misses either target. What type of agreement contains these commitments?
An SLA defines measurable service levels and the remedies if they're missed.
An MOU expresses informal intent, an NDA protects confidential information, and a BPA sets out how business partners operate together.
5.3 Explain the processes associated with third-party risk assessment and management

Before a vendor reviews a company's network diagrams and security architecture during a sales evaluation, the company requires a signed agreement that prohibits the vendor from disclosing that information. Which agreement is this?
An NDA legally protects confidential information shared between parties.
An MOU states intent, a BPA governs a business partnership, and an SOW defines a project's scope and deliverables.
5.3 Explain the processes associated with third-party risk assessment and management

A company already has a master service agreement (MSA) with a consulting firm covering general legal terms. It now needs a document defining the specific deliverables, timeline, and cost of a new penetration test. Which document should be created?
Statement of work (SOW) or work order

An SOW or work order defines the scope, deliverables, schedule, and price of a specific engagement under an existing MSA. An MOU is informal, an SLA sets ongoing service levels, and an NDA protects confidentiality.
5.3 Explain the processes associated with third-party risk assessment and management

Six months after onboarding a payroll vendor, a company reviews the vendor's latest SOC 2 report every year, tracks its external security rating, and watches the news for breaches involving it. What is this activity?
Vendor monitoring continues throughout the relationship, because a vendor's risk changes over time.
Selection and pre-contract due diligence happen before onboarding, and rules of engagement define the scope of security testing.
5.3 Explain the processes associated with third-party risk assessment and management
During vendor selection for a managed security service, it emerges that the procurement lead's brother is a co-owner of one of the bidders. What should the evaluation process identify and address?
A personal relationship that could bias a selection decision is a conflict of interest.
It should be disclosed, and the person removed from the decision, as part of due diligence. There's no service level, audit clause, or MOU involved yet.
5.4 Summarize elements of effective security compliance
A merchant repeatedly fails its PCI DSS assessments and doesn't fix the findings. Which consequence is it most likely to face?
Fines and the possible loss of its ability to process card payments
Non-compliance can lead to fines, sanctions, contract penalties, reputational damage, and the loss of a license or privilege, here the ability to accept cards.
It never brings immunity, lower premiums, or exemption from other laws.
5.4 Summarize elements of effective security compliance

A European customer asks an online retailer to delete all personal data it holds about her. To comply, the retailer must find her data across its CRM, order systems, backups, and marketing tools. Which privacy right is she exercising?
The right to be forgotten (right to erasure)
The right to be forgotten lets data subjects ask for their personal data to be erased, subject to legal exceptions.
It depends on the organization knowing where personal data lives. Portability is about receiving your data, sovereignty concerns jurisdiction, and a legal hold preserves data rather than deleting it.
5.4 Summarize elements of effective security compliance

Every January, each employee must sign a statement confirming they've read and agree to follow the acceptable use and information security policies, and HR stores the records. What is this compliance practice?
Attestation and acknowledgment record that people have read and accepted policies, which supports compliance monitoring and accountability.
Audits, penetration tests, and vendor monitoring are different assurance activities.
5.4 Summarize elements of effective security compliance

A company patches systems promptly, trains staff, and keeps its controls working, acting as a reasonable organization would to protect customer data. Separately, it investigated risks thoroughly before choosing those controls. Which term describes the ongoing responsible implementation of the controls?
Due care is acting responsibly to implement and maintain appropriate protections; due diligence is the research and assessment that informs those choices.

A common shortcut: due diligence is "doing your homework," due care is "doing the right thing" on an ongoing basis. Attestation confirms policy acceptance, and transference shifts risk to another party.
5.4 Summarize elements of effective security compliance
A regional bank must submit an annual certification of its cybersecurity program to the state financial regulator, signed by a senior officer. What type of compliance reporting is this?
Reporting to a regulator or other outside authority is external compliance reporting.
Internal reporting goes to management or the board, a self-assessment may feed the certification but isn't the submission itself, and tabletop exercises test response plans.
5.4 Summarize elements of effective security compliance
To meet privacy obligations, a company needs a maintained record of what personal data it collects, where it's stored, who can access it, and how long it's kept. What is this record?
A data inventory maps personal data and its retention, which is essential for answering data subject requests and proving compliance.
A risk register tracks risks, chain of custody tracks evidence, and an SLA defines service commitments.
5.5 Explain types and purposes of audits and assessments
A company hires testers to simulate an outside attacker. They're given only the company's name, with no network diagrams, credentials, or system details. What type of penetration test is this?
In an unknown environment (black box) test, testers start with little or no information, much like a real external attacker.
A known environment test provides full details, a partially known test provides some, and a defensive test focuses on detection and response.
5.5 Explain types and purposes of audits and assessments
To use the testing budget efficiently, a company gives testers its external IP ranges and one standard employee account, but no architecture documents or source code. What type of test is this?
A partially known environment (gray box) test provides limited information, such as IP ranges or a user account, so testers spend less time on discovery.
A known environment test shares everything, an unknown one shares nothing, and passive reconnaissance is just one phase of testing.
5.5 Explain types and purposes of audits and assessments

Before a penetration test begins, the company and the testing firm sign a document defining which systems are in scope, permitted testing hours, techniques that aren't allowed (such as denial of service), and emergency contacts. What is this document?
Rules of engagement set the boundaries and logistics of a test and provide authorization, protecting both parties.
An NDA covers confidentiality, an SLA sets service levels, and a BPA governs a partnership.
5.5 Explain types and purposes of audits and assessments

At the start of an engagement, testers collect employee names from LinkedIn, find subdomains in public certificate transparency logs, and read the company's job postings to learn its technologies. They don't send any traffic to the company's systems. What phase is this?
Passive reconnaissance gathers information from public sources without interacting with the target's systems.
Active reconnaissance, such as port scanning, touches the target directly, and exploitation and lateral movement come later.
5.5 Explain types and purposes of audits and assessments

A large enterprise customer won't sign a contract with a SaaS provider until the provider shows independent assurance that its security controls operated effectively over the past year. What should the provider supply?
An independent third-party audit report, such as a SOC 2 Type II
An independent third-party audit, such as SOC 2 Type II covering effectiveness over a period, gives external assurance.
Self-assessments, policies, and whitepapers are produced by the provider itself and aren't independent.
5.5 Explain types and purposes of audits and assessments

Instead of running separate exercises, the company's attack simulation team and its SOC work side by side. The attackers run techniques one at a time while the defenders tune detections in real time, and they share findings throughout. What type of penetration testing is this?
Integrated testing (often called purple teaming) combines offensive and defensive work to improve detection and response together.
Purely offensive or defensive tests keep the teams separate, and physical tests target facilities rather than detections.
A company runs monthly simulated phishing campaigns. Which result best shows that its security awareness program is working?
More employees click the links, but fewer report them
The number of campaigns per month goes down
Training completion stays the same while clicks rise
Click rates fall while the share of employees who report suspicious emails rises
Effective awareness both reduces risky actions (clicks) and increases protective ones (reporting), which helps the SOC respond faster.
The other results show worse behavior or say nothing about behavior at all.

An employee accidentally sends a spreadsheet of customer records to the wrong external recipient because the email client auto-completed a similar name. How should this behavior be categorized for awareness training?
Unexpected behavior signalling a compromised account
This was an honest mistake, an unintentional behavior that training and controls such as recipient warnings and DLP can reduce.
Nothing suggests deliberate risk-taking, account compromise, or malicious intent.
Awareness training covers removable media and cables. Which guidance best fits this topic?
Don't plug in USB drives or charging cables you find or receive unexpectedly; hand them to IT or security
Use any free charging kiosk at airports to save battery
Copy work files to personal USB drives so you have a backup
Plug unknown USB drives into a coworker's computer to check what's on them
Unknown USB drives and cables can carry malware or keystroke-injection payloads, so they should be reported rather than used.
Public charging ports can be tampered with, personal USB copies risk data loss, and testing unknown media on another computer just moves the risk.
Many employees now work from coffee shops and shared workspaces. Which training topic best addresses the risks of this setting?
Hybrid and remote work security, such as privacy screens, VPN use, locking devices, and not discussing confidential matters in public
Remote work training covers shoulder surfing, untrusted networks, unattended devices, and overheard conversations.
Data center access, firewall reviews, and change approvals are relevant to IT staff, not the remote workforce's everyday risks.
A person carrying boxes asks an employee to hold the badge-controlled door to the office floor. What does situational awareness training teach the employee to do?
Hold the door, because being helpful matters most
Politely ask the person to badge in or check in at reception, and report it if they refuse
Ignore the person and let the door close without saying anything
Give the person a spare badge
Training teaches employees to recognize tailgating and to respond politely but firmly by directing people to badge in or check in, reporting anyone who won't.
Holding the door enables tailgating, ignoring the person misses a chance to report, and lending badges defeats access control.
A company is redesigning its security awareness program after finding that one annual video isn't changing behavior. Which approach best reflects good program development and execution?
Keep the annual video but make it longer
Replace training with stricter punishments for any mistake
Initial training at onboarding, then recurring, role-specific training with phishing simulations, with results measured and used to adjust the content
Effective programs combine initial and recurring training, tailor content to roles and risks, reinforce it with simulations, and measure results to improve.
A longer annual video, IT-only training, and punishment-focused approaches don't build lasting habits.
A marketing director keeps hearing "AI", "machine learning", and "generative AI" used as if they mean the same thing. Which statement correctly describes how they relate?
Machine learning is a subset of generative AI, which is a subset of AI
Generative AI is a subset of machine learning, which is a subset of AI
AI, machine learning, and generative AI are three separate fields with no overlap
AI is a subset of machine learning that uses rule-based logic
AI is the broad goal of machines doing tasks that need human-like intelligence.

Machine learning is the part of AI where systems learn patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules. Generative AI is a branch of machine learning, built on deep learning and large foundation models, that creates new content such as text, images, or code. The other options reverse or break that hierarchy.

An online retailer's recommendation model was trained last quarter. Every time a shopper opens a product page, the model returns a list of suggested items within milliseconds. What is this step called?
Inference is using an already-trained model to produce outputs from new inputs.

It's the step that runs in production, and it usually drives ongoing cost. Training builds the model from historical data, fine-tuning adapts an existing model with more data, and labeling prepares training data.

A telecom company has five years of customer records. Each record is marked "churned" or "stayed." Leadership wants a model that predicts which current customers are likely to leave. Which learning approach fits?
Supervised learning trains on labeled examples (here, churned or stayed) so it can predict that label for new cases.
Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabeled data, reinforcement learning learns from rewards through trial and error, and rule-based automation doesn't learn from data at all.
A bank wants to discover natural groups among its customers based on spending behavior. It has no predefined segments and no labels. Which approach should the data team use?
With no labels, the goal is to find structure the business doesn't know yet.

Clustering, a form of unsupervised learning, groups similar customers together. Classification and regression are supervised and need known outcomes to learn from, and fine-tuning adapts a pretrained model to a task. It isn't a segmentation method.
A contact center wants to use AI on its call recordings, customer emails, and scanned PDF complaint letters. What type of data are these?
Audio, free text, and scanned documents don't fit neatly into rows and columns, so they're unstructured.

Unstructured data is where generative AI and language models add a lot of value. Structured data lives in tables, time-series data is ordered by time, and "labeled" describes whether known answers are attached, not the format.

A pilot demand-forecasting model performs poorly. The analysis finds duplicate orders, missing store IDs, and two years of data from a product line that was discontinued. What should the business do first?
Switch to a larger, more expensive model
Replace machine learning with generative AI
Clean and curate the training data, then retrain
Deploy the model and let it improve on its own in production
Model quality is limited by data quality: "garbage in, garbage out." Fixing duplicates, gaps, and irrelevant history is the highest-leverage first step.
A bigger model trained on the same flawed data won't fix the root cause, generative AI isn't a forecasting fix, and most models don't improve on their own once deployed.
Which description best fits a foundation model?
A small model built from scratch for one narrow task using company data only
A large model pretrained on broad data that can be adapted to many tasks
A database of approved prompts and responses
A rule engine that encodes a company's business logic
Foundation models, such as the large language models available through Amazon Bedrock, are pretrained on huge, varied datasets.

Businesses adapt them with prompting, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), or fine-tuning instead of building from scratch, which is what makes generative AI fast to adopt. The other options describe narrow models, a prompt library, or a rule engine.
A fraud model gives a transaction a fraud score of 0.82. The operations manager asks what this means for the business. Which response is most accurate?
The transaction is definitely fraudulent and must be blocked
The score has no business meaning until the model is retrained
It's a probability-style estimate; the business must choose a threshold that balances missed fraud against blocking good customers
ML outputs are probabilistic, not certain.

Setting the decision threshold is a business choice. A lower threshold catches more fraud but blocks more legitimate customers (more false positives). A higher threshold lets more fraud through (more false negatives). A single score says nothing about the model's overall accuracy.
A vendor's lead-scoring model is 98% accurate on its training data but only 70% accurate on new leads after go-live. What is the most likely explanation?
Overfitting: the model memorized the training data and doesn't generalize
Underfitting: the model is too simple to learn anything
Hallucination: the model is inventing leads
Inference latency: the model is responding too slowly
High accuracy on training data combined with much lower accuracy on unseen data is the classic sign of overfitting.

Business leaders should ask for performance on held-out or real-world data, not just training results. Underfitting shows poor results on both, hallucination is a generative AI behavior, and latency is about speed, not accuracy.

Which TWO of the following are generative AI use cases? Pick the pair of correct statements.  (1) Drafting first versions of product descriptions for an e-commerce catalog.  (2) Predicting next month's unit sales for each store.  (3) Summarizing a 40-page contract into key obligations.  (4) Flagging emails as spam or not spam.  (5) Scoring loan applicants for default risk.
Generative AI creates new content, such as drafted text or summaries.

Sales forecasting (prediction), spam flagging (classification), and default scoring (risk prediction) are traditional predictive ML tasks. For those tasks, a classic ML model is usually cheaper, more consistent, and easier to explain than a generative model.

A payroll team wants to automate overtime pay. The calculation follows fixed rules set by labor law and company policy, which change about once a year and must be fully auditable. What is the best approach?
Train a machine learning model on past payroll runs
Use rule-based automation that encodes the published rules
Use a generative AI chatbot to calculate each employee's pay
Fine-tune a foundation model on labor law documents
When the logic is known, stable, deterministic, and must be auditable, rule-based automation is cheaper, more predictable, and easier to explain than AI.
ML would only approximate rules that are already known, and generative models can produce inconsistent or wrong numbers. Recognizing when AI is *not* the answer is a core exam theme.
A card issuer's fraud team maintains more than 2,000 hand-written rules. Fraudsters change tactics weekly, and the rules can't keep up. Why is machine learning a better fit here?
ML removes the need for any human fraud analysts
ML is always cheaper than rules
ML can learn complex, changing patterns from data that are impractical to code by hand
ML is valuable when patterns are too complex or change too fast for hand-written rules.
It still needs monitoring, retraining, and human review. No model guarantees zero losses, and ML isn't automatically cheaper, because data, training, and operations all cost money.
A logistics company wants to detect crushed or torn packages automatically from photos taken on the conveyor belt. Which type of AI solution fits?
Computer vision analyzes images and video, for tasks such as defect detection, object recognition, and quality inspection.
NLP works with text and speech, forecasting predicts future values over time, and recommendation systems suggest items to users.
A hotel chain receives 30,000 online reviews a month and wants to know whether guests feel positive or negative about cleanliness, staff, and price. Which AI capability fits?
Sentiment analysis is an NLP task that classifies the emotional tone of text, and it can be broken down by topic.
A pre-trained managed service such as Amazon Comprehend can do this without building a custom model. The other options deal with images, sensor streams, and trial-and-error learning.
A grocery chain wants to estimate how many units of each product every store will sell over the next 8 weeks, accounting for seasonality and holidays. What type of AI solution is this?
Forecasting predicts future numeric values from historical, time-ordered data and accounts for trends and seasonality.
Generative AI creates content, computer vision analyzes images, and clustering groups similar records without predicting the future.

A factory's machines stream temperature and vibration readings every second. The plant manager wants an alert whenever a machine starts behaving unusually, before it fails. Which AI capability fits best?
Anomaly detection learns what normal behavior looks like and flags deviations from it.
It's the basis of predictive maintenance. The other options work on text or create content and don't monitor sensor data.

A lender wants to automate approvals for small-business loans. Regulators require the lender to give every declined applicant specific reasons for the decision. Which consideration should most influence the choice of solution?
Choose whichever model has the highest accuracy, regardless of how it reaches decisions
Use a generative AI model to write a persuasive rejection letter
Prioritize explainability, using an interpretable model or rules so each decision can be justified
Avoid documenting the model's logic to protect intellectual property
When decisions affect people and regulators require reasons, explainability is a hard requirement.

Sometimes it's worth giving up a little accuracy for a model, or a rules-plus-ML approach, whose decisions can be traced. A persuasive letter isn't a real explanation, and hiding the logic undermines compliance and trust.

Which TWO situations are strong signals that AI is NOT the right solution? Pick the pair of correct statements.  (1) The business has years of relevant historical data.  (2) The process has no usable data and none can realistically be collected.  (3) The patterns are complex and change frequently.  (4) The logic is fully known, rarely changes, and errors are unacceptable.  (5) Humans currently do the task but can't keep up with the volume.
AI needs data to learn from, so with no data there's nothing to build on.
When the logic is fully known and must be exact, deterministic rules are better. Plenty of historical data, complex changing patterns, and human tasks that can't scale are all signals in favor of AI.
An accounts-payable team wants to pull vendor names, totals, and due dates from thousands of PDF invoices. They have no data scientists. Which approach is most appropriate?
Use a pre-trained, managed AI service built for document extraction
Hire a team to build and train a custom computer vision model from scratch
Fine-tune a large language model on the company's entire file share
Keep entering the invoices manually because AI requires data scientists
Common tasks like invoice extraction are well served by pre-trained AI services (for example, Amazon Textract) that need no ML expertise and deliver value quickly.
Building from scratch or fine-tuning adds cost, time, and risk without a clear benefit. Not having data scientists doesn't rule AI out.
An insurer's claims leader asks for "generative AI to estimate the dollar cost of each new auto claim." What should an AI business strategist recommend?
Use generative AI, because it can handle any kind of AI task
Treat it as a predictive (regression) problem and consider a traditional ML model, possibly with generative AI to summarize claim notes
Avoid AI entirely, because claims involve money
Use computer vision alone, because cost estimates come only from photos
Estimating a number from historical outcomes is a prediction (regression) task, where traditional ML tends to be more accurate, consistent, cheaper, and easier to explain.
Generative AI can still add value alongside it, for example by summarizing adjuster notes. Matching the type of AI to the problem, not to the hype, is what this exam tests.
A COO asks how an "AI agent" differs from the FAQ chatbot already on the company website. Which answer is most accurate?
An agent is a chatbot with a more natural-sounding voice
An agent only works with structured data, while chatbots use text
An agent can plan multi-step tasks and take actions in other systems using tools, not just answer questions
An agent is a chatbot that never needs human oversight
The defining traits of an agent are a goal, the ability to plan steps, and tool use.

For example, an agent can look up an order, issue a return label, and update the CRM. A chatbot responds to questions. Voice and data type don't define an agent, and agents need *more* oversight than chatbots, not less, because they take actions.
A retailer is deploying a customer-service agent that can issue refunds. Leadership wants speed but is worried about large mistakes. Which design best balances value and risk?
Let the agent refund up to a set limit on its own and require human approval above that limit
Let the agent issue any refund on its own to maximize speed
Require human approval for every refund, including $3 ones
Don't allow agents near financial actions under any circumstances
Matching how much the agent can do alone to the risk of the action is the core agent-governance principle.

Low-value, reversible actions can be automated, and high-impact ones need a human in the loop. Full autonomy takes on unnecessary risk, approving every refund wipes out the value, and a blanket ban gives up a sound use case.
A sales assistant agent must check live inventory in the company's ERP system before it quotes delivery dates. What capability makes this possible?
Fine-tuning the model on last year's inventory data
Tool use, also called function calling, through an approved API to the ERP
Agents reach live systems by calling tools such as APIs, databases, and business applications.
A context window holds text the model is given, not live data. Fine-tuning on old inventory would produce stale answers, and temperature controls how varied the wording is.

An insurer designs a claims process in which one supervisor agent hands work to a document-extraction agent, a policy-check agent, and a fraud-screening agent, then assembles their results. What is this pattern called?
Orchestration coordinates specialized agents, each with a narrow job, under a supervisor or workflow.

Specialized agents are easier to test, govern, and improve than one do-everything agent. RAG is a retrieval technique, continued pre-training is a model customization method, and rule-based automation doesn't involve agents.

An email-triage agent can read incoming messages and send emails on staff's behalf. A security review finds that a malicious incoming email could contain hidden instructions telling the agent to forward confidential files outside the company. Which response best addresses this risk?
Raise the model's temperature so it ignores instructions
Shut down all AI use in the company
Limit the agent's permissions to what it needs, add guardrails, and require human approval before it sends sensitive data externally
Fine-tune the model on more email examples
This is prompt injection, which is especially dangerous for agents that can take actions.

Layered controls reduce both the chance of an attack succeeding and the damage it can do: least privilege, input and output guardrails, and approval steps for high-impact actions. Temperature and fine-tuning don't address the threat, and a blanket shutdown is disproportionate.

An HR team wants employees to get instant answers about the benefits handbook. Nothing in the process needs to be changed in other systems. A vendor proposes an autonomous multi-agent platform. What should an AI business strategist recommend?
Accept the multi-agent platform, because agents are the newest technology
Build a custom foundation model for HR
Use rule-based automation, because AI can't answer questions
Start with a simpler generative AI assistant grounded in the handbook (RAG), and add agent capabilities only if actions are needed later
Agents add complexity, cost, and risk that are only justified when the task needs actions or multi-step work.

Answering questions from documents is a classic RAG job. The exam rewards choosing the simplest option that meets the need, not the newest technology. A custom model is overkill, and rules can't handle open-ended questions well.

A bank is about to launch an agent that updates customer records. Which TWO controls should be in place before go-live? Pick the pair of correct statements.  (1) Detailed logs of every action the agent takes, for audit and investigation.  (2) Administrator-level access to all systems so the agent never gets blocked.  (3) Turning off logging to reduce response time.  (4) Letting the agent choose its own permissions as needed.  (5) Least-privilege access limited to the records and actions the use case requires.
Audit trails make agent actions traceable and accountable, and least privilege limits the damage if the agent errs or is manipulated.
Broad admin access, self-assigned permissions, and turning off logging all increase risk and weaken governance.
A travel company's booking agent will remember each customer's seat and meal preferences across future conversations. Which business consideration does this memory feature raise most directly?
The need for a larger GPU cluster
Data privacy, consent, and retention policies for stored customer information
Removing the need for a privacy notice
Agent memory is stored personal data.

The business needs a lawful basis or consent, clear retention limits, a way for customers to delete their data, and access controls. Hardware and learning type aren't the issue, and memory makes a privacy notice *more* necessary, not less.
A manufacturer's procurement agent will negotiate routine reorders directly with suppliers' AI agents. What should leadership define before allowing this agent-to-agent interaction?
Authority limits (spend caps, approved suppliers, contract terms), escalation rules, and who is accountable for agreed outcomes
Nothing, because agents negotiating with agents carry no business risk
A policy that suppliers must use the same AI vendor
When agents act for the business with outside parties, governance has to define what the agent may commit to, when a person takes over, and who owns the result.
Agent-to-agent deals create real contractual and financial exposure. Temperature is a minor technical setting, and requiring the same vendor isn't realistic or relevant.
A marketing team's generative AI drafts are too formal and don't follow the brand's style. What should the team try first?
Fine-tune a model on 10,000 brand documents
Improve the prompts with clear tone instructions, brand rules, and a few sample outputs
Build a custom model from scratch
Prompt engineering is the cheapest and fastest way to customize a model, so it comes first.
Instructions, a system prompt with brand rules, and examples often fix tone. Fine-tuning and custom models cost far more and are justified only if better prompting falls short.
An analyst includes three example customer emails, each paired with an ideal reply, in the prompt before asking the model to reply to a new email. What technique is this?
Few-shot prompting puts a handful of examples in the prompt to show the desired format and style.
Zero-shot gives no examples. Fine-tuning changes the model itself through further training, and RAG retrieves documents for content rather than providing worked examples.

A legal-ops team pastes an entire 200-page contract into every question it asks a generative AI tool, and the monthly bill is far higher than expected. The service charges per input and output token. Which change would cut cost the most while keeping answers useful?
Send only the relevant sections, for example by retrieving passages with RAG, instead of the whole contract each time
Token-based pricing means input size drives cost.
Sending only the relevant passages cuts tokens sharply and often improves focus. Longer prompts and larger models raise cost, and temperature has no effect on token pricing.
A field-service company wants technicians to ask questions about a 600-page equipment manual. The manual is longer than the model's context window. What is the most practical approach?
Use RAG to retrieve and send only the manual sections relevant to each question
Wait for a model with an unlimited context window
Train a new foundation model on the manual
The context window caps how much text a model can consider at once.

RAG works around it by indexing the manual, often as embeddings in a vector store, and retrieving only the relevant chunks per question. Waiting or cutting the manual isn't practical, and training a foundation model is extremely costly and unnecessary.

A bank's internal assistant must answer staff questions about lending policies. The policies change weekly, and compliance requires every answer to show which policy document it came from. Which approach fits best?
Fine-tune the model on the policies every week
Use a general model with no access to the policies
Use retrieval-augmented generation over the current policy library, with citations
Use continued pre-training on banking textbooks
RAG pulls current documents at question time, so updates take effect without retraining, and answers can cite their sources, which compliance needs.
Weekly fine-tuning is costly and can't easily cite sources. A general model doesn't know internal policies, and textbooks don't contain this bank's rules.

A medical-coding vendor needs a model to produce outputs in a highly specialized format and terminology across millions of records. Careful prompting and examples still give inconsistent formatting. The underlying knowledge rarely changes, and the vendor has thousands of high-quality labeled examples. What is the most appropriate next step?
Switch to RAG, because RAG fixes formatting
Fine-tune a foundation model on the labeled examples
Raise the temperature for more variety
Fine-tuning fits when you need consistent *behavior*, such as format, style, or domain-specific output, that prompting can't deliver, and you have quality labeled data.
RAG adds knowledge rather than shaping behavior, higher temperature makes outputs less consistent, and going back to manual coding gives up the efficiency gains.
A customer-service chatbot confidently tells a customer about a "60-day no-questions-asked refund policy." The company has never offered such a policy. What is this called?
A hallucination is a fluent, confident output that's false or made up.

It can create legal and reputational exposure, as when a company is held to a chatbot's invented policy. Drift is decay over time, overfitting is a training problem, and prompt injection is a malicious input attack.
A compliance team uses generative AI to summarize regulatory filings. They want summaries that are consistent and factual, not creative, each time. Which setting adjustment helps most?
Lower temperature makes outputs more predictable and focused, which suits factual and compliance tasks.
Higher temperature adds variety and creativity, which suits brainstorming. Output length doesn't control consistency, and removing the system prompt takes away useful instructions.
Which sequence correctly orders generative AI customization approaches from least to most effort and cost?
Fine-tuning → RAG → prompt engineering → continued pre-training
RAG → prompt engineering → continued pre-training → fine-tuning
Prompt engineering → RAG → fine-tuning → continued pre-training
Continued pre-training → fine-tuning → RAG → prompt engineering

RAG adds a retrieval system but no training. Fine-tuning needs labeled data and training runs, and continued pre-training needs large volumes of domain text and the most compute. The business rule is to stop at the cheapest rung that meets the need.

A healthcare provider is launching a patient-facing assistant and wants to reduce the risk of made-up answers. Which TWO measures are most effective? Pick the pair of correct statements.  (1) Raise the temperature so the model explores more answers.  (2) Ground responses in approved clinical content using RAG.  (3) Remove the system prompt so the model is less constrained.  (4) Require citations and route uncertain or sensitive answers to human review.  (5) Encourage longer, more creative responses.
Grounding in trusted content and adding verification steps, such as citations and human escalation, are the main hallucination controls.
Higher temperature, fewer instructions, and longer creative answers all *increase* the chance of fabricated content.
A sales team complains that the company's generative AI assistant "doesn't know" about a product launched last month and asks IT to "fix the bug." What is the most accurate explanation and fix?
The model is broken and must be replaced with a different vendor's model
The model's training data ends before the launch (its knowledge cutoff); supply current product information through RAG or the prompt
The context window is too large, so the model ignored the product
The model has drifted, so it must be fully retrained from scratch every month
Foundation models know only what was in their training data up to a cutoff date.

That's expected behavior, not a bug. The practical fix is to provide current, company-specific information at query time through RAG or the prompt. Switching vendors doesn't solve it, a large context window isn't the cause, and monthly retraining from scratch is impractical.

A subscription company's churn model was accurate at launch. Over nine months, after a competitor entered the market, its predictions became steadily less reliable, even though no one changed the model. What is happening, and what's the right response?
Model drift; monitor performance against a baseline and retrain on recent data
Model drift is performance decay as the real world moves away from the training data.

The response is ongoing monitoring with alert thresholds and periodic retraining. Deployed AI is never "done." Hallucination and prompt injection are generative AI issues, and overfitting shows up at launch, not gradually.
A bank's credit model was trained mostly on applicants aged 35–60. After a campaign aimed at university students, most new applicants are 18–24. Model accuracy drops. What type of drift is this?
Data drift means the incoming data no longer looks like the training data, here because the applicant population changed.
Concept drift is when the relationship between inputs and outcomes changes. Hallucination is a generative AI behavior, and underfitting is a training-time weakness.
A payments company's fraud model sees the same kinds of transactions as before. But fraudsters have changed tactics, so patterns that used to be safe are now often fraudulent. What is this called?
Concept drift is a change in the *relationship* between inputs and the correct outcome, even when the inputs look similar.
It's common in fraud and security, where adversaries adapt. Data drift is a change in the inputs themselves. Overfitting and versioning are different concepts.
An internal audit finds employees pasting customer contracts into free, personal generative AI websites to summarize them. What is the most effective response?
Ignore it, because employees are being productive
Block all AI websites permanently and stop discussing AI
Provide an approved, secure enterprise AI tool, publish an acceptable use policy, and train staff on what data may be used
This is shadow AI, and it signals real demand that the business isn't meeting.

Bans alone push usage further underground. The effective response channels the demand into a governed tool, sets clear rules, and teaches people why. Ignoring it risks data leakage, and punishment without alternatives damages trust.

A generative AI customer-support assistant has been live for three months. Which TWO should the business monitor on an ongoing basis? Pick the pair of correct statements.  (1) Output quality, such as accuracy, groundedness, and customer satisfaction, compared with the launch baseline.  (2) The font used in the assistant's chat window.  (3) Usage and cost trends, such as token consumption and cost per resolved conversation.  (4) Nothing, because generative AI models don't change once deployed.  (5) The number of vendor press releases about new models.
Ongoing monitoring covers quality and safety (does it still work well?) and economics (is it still worth it?).
Quality can shift as content, users, and vendor models change, and costs can grow with usage. Fonts and press releases aren't operational metrics, and "set and forget" is never right for AI.
Agents using an internal knowledge assistant can rate answers with a thumbs up or down and type in corrections. How does this feature create business value over time?
It replaces the need for any governance
It creates a feedback loop that shows where prompts, source documents, or retrieval need improving
It automatically retrains the foundation model every night
User feedback shows where the system fails, for example missing or outdated documents or weak prompts, so the team can prioritize fixes and measure improvement.
It doesn't replace governance, doesn't by itself retrain a foundation model, and has no effect on pricing.
A new Chief AI Officer suspects many departments are using AI tools that haven't been approved, but no one knows which tools or what data they touch. What should come first?
Publish a strict policy banning all unapproved tools immediately
Buy an enterprise license for one tool and require everyone to switch the next day
Discover and catalog the AI tools in use, the data they handle, and their owners (an AI inventory)
Wait for a data incident to reveal which tools are risky
You can't govern what you can't see.

An AI inventory shows the actual usage, the risks, and the unmet needs, which then shape sensible policies and approved alternatives. Banning or switching tools before understanding the situation causes disruption, and waiting for an incident is negligent.

A company's marketing assistant suddenly writes noticeably different copy. The cause: the model provider released a new model version, and the application automatically switched to it. Which practice would have prevented the surprise?
Pinning a specific model version and evaluating new versions against test cases before adopting them
Version pinning plus evaluation before rollout keeps model upgrades deliberate and tested.
It's the generative AI version of change management. Temperature affects randomness, not versions. Removing monitoring makes things worse, and rules can't write marketing copy.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
A regional bank's board asks leadership for an AI strategy. Where should the strategy start?
With the bank's business goals and biggest problems, then identifying where AI can move those outcomes
With a list of the newest foundation models
With copying a competitor's announced AI projects
With buying GPUs so the bank is ready for anything
Good AI strategy is business strategy first: start from goals such as growth, cost, risk, or customer experience, and work back to AI opportunities.
Model lists, copying competitors, and buying infrastructure first are technology-led and usually produce pilots with no clear value.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
A strategist is mapping AI capabilities to business outcomes for an insurance claims department. Which statement is the best capability-to-outcome mapping?
"We will use a large language model because it's state of the art."
"Document summarization will cut adjuster reading time per claim, lowering handling cost per claim and speeding settlement."
"We will deploy agents in every department by Q3."
A strong mapping traces the chain from capability (summarization) to an operational effect (less reading time) to measurable business outcomes (cost per claim, cycle time).
The other statements name technology or ambition without a measurable outcome.

A 300-person logistics firm has no data scientists and a modest IT budget. It wants to use AI to reduce invoice processing time and improve customer email response. Which strategic approach best fits its resources?
Hire a 15-person ML research team to build proprietary models
Train its own foundation model to create a competitive moat
Postpone AI until it can afford a data science team
Favor managed AI services and ready-made solutions for these common needs, building only where it differentiates

Invoice extraction and email assistance are common needs that managed services and SaaS handle well, with fast time to value and no ML team. Building research teams or foundation models doesn't fit the firm's scale, and waiting gives up achievable value.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation

A retailer's AI steering committee has approved eight initiatives. All eight are multi-year, high-risk transformation bets, and none are expected to show results within 12 months. What is the main strategic concern?
The portfolio lacks quick wins that build momentum, prove value, and keep sponsor support
High-risk bets should never be funded
Results within 12 months are impossible with AI
A healthy AI portfolio balances quick wins, which show early value and build skills and credibility, with strategic bets for long-term advantage.
An all-bets portfolio risks losing executive support before anything pays off. Strategic bets are fine in moderation, and many AI uses deliver value quickly.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation

Procurement approvals at a manufacturer take 15 days. Analysis shows each request passes through five sequential sign-offs, three of which duplicate checks already done. A vendor proposes an AI agent to "speed up approvals." What should the strategist recommend first?
Deploy the AI agent across all five sign-offs
Redesign the process to remove redundant steps, then decide whether AI adds value to what remains
Fine-tune a model on past approval emails
Add a sixth AI review step to improve quality
Automating a broken process just makes waste faster.

The root cause is process design, not missing intelligence. Recognizing when AI isn't the (first) answer is an explicit exam theme. After simplifying the process, AI may still help, for example by pre-checking requests.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation

A hospital wants to reduce nurses' documentation burden. One option is to have AI write and file nursing notes with no human review. Another is to have AI draft the notes for nurses to review and sign. Which is the stronger strategic choice, and why?
Full automation, because it saves the most time in theory
Neither, because healthcare can't use AI
AI drafts with nurse review, because augmentation captures most of the time savings while keeping clinical accountability and building trust
Full automation, because nurses will resist any change anyway
In high-stakes settings, augmenting people (AI drafts, a human decides) usually gives the best balance of value, safety, accountability, and adoption.
Full automation of clinical records raises patient-safety and liability risk. Healthcare uses AI widely, and assuming resistance isn't a strategy.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
Which element is most essential to include when an AI initiative is approved as part of the strategy?
The name of the foundation model to be used
A measurable business outcome, its KPIs and baseline, and an accountable business owner
Without a defined outcome, a baseline, KPIs, and an owner, you can't judge success or decide whether to scale or stop.
Model choice is a later technical decision, vendor materials aren't a plan, and no AI system can promise 100% accuracy.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation

Which TWO inputs are most important for aligning an AI strategy with the organization? Pick the pair of correct statements.  (1) The latest public model benchmark leaderboard.  (2) The organization's strategic goals and priorities.  (3) A vendor's suggested list of AI products.  (4) Customer needs and pain points.  (5) The number of AI press releases competitors issued this year.
Alignment means connecting AI to what the organization is trying to achieve and what its customers need.
Benchmarks, vendor product lists, and competitor press releases may inform later choices, but they don't define strategic direction.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
A company debates who should own its AI strategy. The CIO wants IT to own it, and business unit heads want to run their own AI plans independently. Which ownership model is most effective?
Joint ownership: business leaders accountable for outcomes, partnering with technology, data, and risk leaders, under an executive sponsor
IT alone, because AI is a technology
Each business unit alone, with no coordination
The AI vendor, because it knows the technology best
AI value is realized in business processes, but it depends on shared platforms, data, security, and governance.

Effective strategy is co-owned and sponsored at the executive level. IT alone loses business focus, uncoordinated units duplicate effort and risk, and outsourcing the strategy to a vendor creates conflicts of interest.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation

A company wrote a detailed three-year AI strategy two years ago and hasn't revisited it. Since then, model capabilities have improved dramatically, prices have dropped, and two of its planned custom builds are now available as low-cost managed services. What does this situation show?
Strategies should never be written down
The original strategy was correct and must be followed to the end
AI strategy should be a living plan, reviewed regularly so priorities, build/buy choices, and investments can be adjusted
The company should stop using AI until the market stabilizes
The AI landscape moves fast, so strategy needs regular reviews (for example quarterly) to reprioritize, switch builds to buys, and reallocate funding.
Following an outdated plan wastes money, and pausing gives up value. Writing a strategy down is fine; the mistake is never updating it.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation

A distributor is picking its first generative AI pilot. Option 1 is AI-driven dynamic pricing: very high potential value, but pricing data is scattered across five systems and needs a year of cleanup. Option 2 is AI drafting answers to sales-rep product questions from an existing, well-maintained product catalog: moderate value, data ready, low risk. Which should be the first pilot?
Option 1, because the highest value always goes first
Option 2, because it combines solid value with high feasibility and low risk, making it a good first win
Neither, until all data across the company is perfect
Both at once, with equal funding
Use-case evaluation weighs value against feasibility (especially data readiness), risk, and time to value.

A feasible, moderate-value pilot builds capability and credibility. The pricing initiative can start its data foundation work in parallel. Waiting for perfect data stalls progress, and splitting focus raises risk.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
An HR team proposes AI to automatically screen out job applicants. The projected time savings are large. How should this use case be evaluated compared with an AI tool that drafts job descriptions?
Identically, since both are HR use cases
Approve the screening tool first, because it saves more time
Reject both, because HR data is sensitive
Treat the screening tool as higher risk, because it affects people's access to jobs, and require bias testing, explainability, human review, and legal input before approval
Use-case evaluation must weigh risk, not just value.

Automated decisions about people's employment are high-risk, and regulations such as the EU AI Act classify them that way, so they need much stronger controls. Drafting job descriptions is lower risk, with a person reviewing the output. Rejecting all HR AI is overly cautious.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
A transformation office plots candidate AI use cases on a value-versus-feasibility matrix. Which quadrant holds the "quick wins" to pursue first?
Quick wins deliver meaningful value and are easy to execute because data, skills, and integration are ready.
High-value, low-feasibility items are strategic bets that need deliberate investment. Low-value, high-feasibility items are "maybe later." Low-value, low-feasibility items should be dropped.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
A two-week proof of concept shows that a generative AI model can draft accurate responses to warranty claims using the company's data. What is the most appropriate next step?
Roll out to all 2,000 service agents next Monday
Run a pilot with a limited group of real users, measuring agreed business KPIs against a baseline
Declare success and close the project
Start a second proof of concept with a different model
A proof of concept proves technical feasibility ("can it work?").

A pilot proves business value and adoption ("does it deliver results with real users?"). Jumping straight to full rollout skips that test. Stopping after the proof of concept captures no value, and another proof of concept delays learning.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
Before launching a 90-day pilot of an AI sales-forecasting tool, the sponsor asks how the team will decide whether to scale it. What should be agreed before the pilot starts?
Nothing; the team will decide based on how users feel at the end
The model the vendor will use in two years
Measurable success criteria and thresholds for scale, iterate, or stop decisions, plus the baseline to compare against
A promise that the pilot will be scaled no matter what
Criteria agreed in advance, such as a forecast error reduction of at least X% or a weekly adoption rate of at least Y%, prevent goalposts from moving and allow objective stage-gate decisions.
Gut feel invites bias, future model plans are irrelevant, and guaranteeing a scale-up defeats the purpose of a pilot.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation

A pilot has run for six months and gone through two rounds of improvements. Adoption is still 12%, against a target of 60%, and measured savings are a fraction of the business case. The team argues for more funding because "we've already spent $400,000." What should the steering committee do?
Approve more funding, because stopping would waste the $400,000
Scale it company-wide to increase adoption
Keep running it indefinitely without new targets
Stop the initiative, capture the lessons, and reallocate funding to stronger use cases
Money already spent shouldn't drive future decisions; that's the sunk cost fallacy.

When a pilot repeatedly misses its pre-agreed criteria, a disciplined portfolio stops it and moves the funds. Scaling a failing pilot spreads the failure, and running it with no targets is how "pilot purgatory" happens.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation

A pilot of AI-assisted patient triage is meeting all its quality and value targets. However, the national regulator has announced new guidance for AI in triage, due in four months, and the requirements aren't yet known. What is the most sensible portfolio decision?
Scale nationwide immediately before the rules arrive
Pause scaling, keep the pilot's learnings and assets, and resume once the guidance is clear
Ignore the regulator, because the pilot is working
Portfolio decisions include scale, iterate, *pause*, and stop.

Pausing fits when the use case works but an external factor, here regulatory uncertainty, makes scaling risky right now. Terminating throws away proven value, and rushing ahead or ignoring the regulator creates compliance risk.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
A pilot of an AI writing assistant for the support team met every success criterion: 70% weekly adoption, 25% faster resolution, and satisfaction scores holding steady. What should come next?
Scale in phases to more teams, with monitoring, training, and support in place
Stop the initiative, because pilots are only experiments
Start over with a new proof of concept
Remove the success metrics now that the pilot is done
Meeting criteria agreed in advance triggers the decision to scale.

Phased scaling, with monitoring and change support, manages risk while capturing value. Stopping or restarting wastes proven results, and metrics should continue into production to confirm the value holds.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation

When assessing a use case's feasibility, which TWO factors matter most? Pick the pair of correct statements.  (1) Whether the needed data exists, is accessible, and is of sufficient quality.  (2) How many press articles mention the use case.  (3) Whether the CEO has used generative AI personally.  (4) Whether the skills and system integrations required are available or obtainable.  (5) How futuristic the use case sounds.
Feasibility depends on practical delivery factors: data readiness, and the skills, tools, and integrations needed to put the solution into real workflows.
Press coverage, an executive's personal experience, and novelty don't make a use case easier to deliver.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
Which is the best-defined AI use case statement?
"Help accounts-payable clerks extract invoice data automatically, reducing average processing time from 9 minutes to under 3 minutes per invoice within six months."
A good use case names the users, the problem, and a measurable outcome with a baseline, a target, and a timeframe.
The other statements are vague ambitions or technology choices with no way to measure success.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation

Over two years, a company has launched 14 AI pilots. Each impressed at demo day, but none reached production. Interviews show the pilots had no named business owners, no agreed success criteria, and no budget or plan for production. What best describes the problem and the fix?
Model quality; switch to a larger foundation model
The technology isn't ready; wait two more years
Pilot purgatory; require a business owner, success criteria, and a funded path to production before any pilot is approved
Pilot purgatory comes from weak governance and planning, not weak technology.

Fixing the approval process, with an owner, criteria, and a scale plan up front, turns experiments into value. Bigger models and more pilots repeat the pattern, and the evidence shows the technology works at demo level.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation

A company ranks AI use cases with a weighted scorecard covering value, feasibility, strategic fit, and risk. A proposal to use AI to set individual insurance premiums automatically, with no human review, scores highest overall. But the legal team rates its compliance risk as "unacceptable" under current regulations. What should happen?
Approve it, because it has the highest total score
Average the legal concern into the score and proceed if it still ranks first
Don't approve it in its current form; treat unacceptable risk as a gate that a high score can't override, and consider redesigning it, for example with human review
Hide the legal rating from the steering committee
Some criteria act as gates rather than weights.

Unacceptable legal or ethical risk stops a use case no matter how valuable it is. Redesigning it with human oversight, explainability, and compliant data use may bring it within risk tolerance. Averaging the risk away or hiding the rating undermines governance.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation

A mid-size company wants an AI assistant that answers routine employee IT and HR questions. Many proven SaaS products already do this, and it isn't a competitive differentiator. What's the most sensible approach?
Build a custom solution from scratch with a new data science team
Buy a proven solution and configure it with the company's content
Partner with a university on a multi-year research project
For commodity needs, buying gives the fastest time to value and the lowest risk.

"Build core, buy context": save custom building for what differentiates the business. Building from scratch, training a foundation model, or a research partnership all cost far more than this need justifies.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation

A specialty insurer has 30 years of proprietary claims and underwriting data. Its pricing accuracy is its main competitive advantage, and it has an experienced data science team. It wants AI to improve risk pricing. Which approach fits best?
Build a custom solution on a managed ML platform using its proprietary data
Buy the same off-the-shelf pricing tool its competitors use
Avoid AI to protect its data
Let a vendor own the pricing model and the data
Build when the capability is a core differentiator, the company has unique data, and it has the skills.

A managed platform such as Amazon SageMaker AI reduces the infrastructure burden. Buying the competitors' tool erases the advantage, avoiding AI gives up value, and handing over the model and data loses control of the core asset.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation

A regional retailer wants a generative AI shopping assistant in production within four months for the holiday season. It has strong product data but no in-house AI experience, and hiring would take six months. What's the best approach?
Build it with the existing web team learning as they go
Partner with an experienced AWS Partner to deliver, and include knowledge transfer to build internal skills
Partnering fills skill gaps and speeds delivery when the timeline is tight.

Building knowledge transfer into the engagement reduces long-term dependence on the partner. Waiting misses the season, learning on the job risks quality and timing, and cancelling gives up a viable opportunity.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation

A legal-services firm wants a research assistant grounded in its proprietary case library. It doesn't want to train its own models but does want to control its data and workflow. Which approach best describes this?
Pure buy: a generic consumer chatbot
Pure build: train its own large language model
Hybrid: use managed foundation models (for example, through Amazon Bedrock) and build its own retrieval layer and workflow on its proprietary data
Pure partner: outsource all legal research to a vendor
The hybrid approach is common: buy or rent the commodity layer (foundation models) and build the differentiating layer (proprietary data, RAG, workflow, user experience).
A consumer chatbot lacks control and grounding, training a model from scratch is wasteful, and outsourcing everything gives away the firm's differentiator.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation

Option 1, building in-house, has an estimated development cost of $150,000. Option 2, a SaaS subscription, costs $90,000 a year. The CFO is leaning toward building because "$150,000 once is cheaper than $90,000 every year." What should the analysis compare?
Total cost of ownership over the expected lifetime, including hosting, maintenance, staff, monitoring, upgrades, and opportunity cost
Build costs continue well after launch: infrastructure, maintenance engineers, model updates, security, and monitoring.
Comparing total cost of ownership, plus time to value, gives a fair answer. Sticker prices, discounts alone, and how innovative an option sounds lead to poor decisions.
